TRK-001

CUBESAT-1U

Vehicle · in view of GND-01 · ALERT

Pi header pins 3 and 5 are dead

GPIO2 and GPIO3 no longer work open-drain. They still read high, drive as outputs, and measure 3.27 V on a meter — which is exactly why four scans, two custom scripts and a full software audit all missed it. Nothing ever acknowledges on them.

I²C runs on a software bus instead: dtoverlay=i2c-gpio,i2c_gpio_sda=23,i2c_gpio_scl=24,bus=3 — that is pins 16 and 18, and i2cdetect must be given -y 3. If the SD card is ever reflashed, that line has to go back or it will look like a brand-new fault.

The rule the flight agent must respect

Glide, never jump, and release after every move. Eased motion never asks a motor for full speed from rest, which is why both wings can move together on one cell against the original one-at-a-time rule. The ±60° reboot came from holding position back to back — duty cycle matters more than angle.

CubeSat · Pi Zero 2 W

Project pinout

Pick a component and the wires are drawn from the Pi's pins to it. Tap any individual pin for detail. Selecting PCA9685 and then SENSORS shows the same four pins lighting up twice — that is I²C being a shared bus.

Chain, not a star. Pi → PCA9685 (Dupont, working) → its bare 6-pin header (4 soldered wires) → Qwiic pHAT → BME280 → IMU. The Pi’s four I²C wires go to the PCA9685 only; everything downstream hangs off that.
3.3 V 5 V Ground I²C SPI EEPROM unused
Pins 3 and 5 are damaged on this Pi. The hardware I²C peripheral no longer works open-drain — the pins still drive as outputs, which is why they measure and toggle correctly, but nothing ever acknowledges. Proven by moving the same board and wires to bit-banged pins, where 0x40 appeared instantly. I²C now runs on pins 16 and 18 as a software bus (bus 3), set in config.txt.
Pins 27 and 28 are the HAT EEPROM bus. Leave them alone — a HAT reads its identity from there at boot.

CubeSat · Bench Bring-up

Breadboard test guide

Everything here runs without the Qwiic pHAT. The Pi's hammer-header pins take female jumpers directly, so the breadboard stands in for it. Build with power off, test one subsystem at a time.

This Pi's hardware I²C is dead — use pins 16 and 18

GPIO2 and GPIO3 (pins 3 and 5) took 5 V twice and no longer work open-drain. They still measure and toggle correctly, which is exactly why it was hard to find. I²C runs as a software bus on pins 16 and 18 now, and i2cdetect must be given -y 3.

Read before powering anything

3.3 V and 5 V must never touch. A 5 V wire that slipped onto a 3.3 V pad is what destroyed the last pHAT and the BME280 with it. Trace both rails end to end with your eyes before the switch goes on — every single time you change the wiring.

The Pi's header

Every pin, with the ten you use highlighted and labelled with where they go. Pin 1 is the square solder pad on the underside — all the others are round — at the end nearest the microSD slot.

Pins 27 and 28 are the HAT EEPROM bus (amber). Never use them for anything. Every unhighlighted pin stays empty.

Stage 1 — the servo driver

Look at your board. It has four separate areas, and only three of them you touch.

The servo plugs — just match the colours

Your MG90S plug has three wires: orange, red, brown. The board's pins are yellow, red, black. Line them up in that order — orange onto yellow, red onto red, brown onto black — and it's right. You do not need to count pins or read silkscreen.

The picture — where each wire goes

Pi on the left with its header running down the edge. Where two wires cross, the one on top is drawn over the other.

3.3 V — chip 5 V — servos GND SDA SCL

Wires 1–4 · to the 6-pin header

These four make the board talk. Straight across, no crossings — the order below matches the order the pins appear on the board.

Wires 5–6 · to the green screw terminal

These two make the servos move. A completely separate supply — this is the step people skip.

Purple is 3.3 V. Red is 5 V. They are not interchangeable.

Purple (Pi pin 1) goes to VCC and powers the chip. Red (Pi pin 2) goes to the screw terminal and powers the servos. Putting 5 V on VCC is how the last board died.

From Pi pinTo PCA9685Why
11 — 3.3 VVCCpowers the chip
26 — GNDGNDsignal ground
316 — SDASDAdata
418 — SCLSCLclock
52 — 5 Vscrew terminal +powers the servos
69 — GNDscrew terminal −servo ground

The two wires people forget are 5 and 6

Wires 1–4 make the board talk. Wires 5–6 make the servos move. They are separate supplies. Fit only 1–4 and i2cdetect finds the board at 0x40, your code runs with no errors, and the servos barely twitch.

OE is the sixth pin on that header — leave it empty. The screw terminal takes bare wire: strip 7 mm, twist, tighten, then tug to check.

Stage 2 — LED strip

Only after stage 1 passes. Four wires, and the strip's 5 V is the most dangerous wire on the bench.

Pi pinSignalStrip pad
2 or 45 V5V
20GNDG
19MOSID — data
23SCKC — clock

Three things that make a working strip look dead

Wrong end — arrows point away from where data enters; connect the tail, not the head. No shared ground — data and clock are meaningless without it. Only 12 LEDs lit — the test defaults to 12 of your 144, at the input end; run bench.py led 144.

No level shifter

Your HiLetgo is a bidirectional I²C type, good to a few hundred kHz. This bus runs at 1–2 MHz and it would corrupt the signal rather than help. SK9822 accepts 3.3 V logic directly — drive it straight from the Pi.

Complete wiring layout

Every component and every connection in the satellite. Solid = plug or screw. Dashed = soldered. Numbers on the wires are Pi header pins.

3.3 V 5 V GND SDA / I²C SCL MOSI SCK servo

Dashed wires are the only soldering — four male header pins into the PCA9685’s bare 6-pin footprint. Everything else is a plug, a screw terminal, or a Dupont jumper.

PCA9685 → Qwiic pHAT

Four wires. Not six. V+ and OE stay empty.

Never put V+ on a Qwiic bus

V+ is the 5 V servo supply from the green screw terminal. Qwiic is a 3.3 V bus. Connect them and you feed 5 V straight into the BME280 and the IMU, which is the same failure that already destroyed one sensor. V+ and OE get nothing.

Yes, you need GND — it is one of the four. Ground is the reference the data and clock lines are measured against, not just a power return. Without it the bus cannot work even with the other three perfect.

Solder the cut Qwiic cable's four wires directly into holes 2, 3, 4 and 6. Tin each wire first so it behaves like a solid pin instead of fraying. The other end plugs into any port on the pHAT — all four ports are the same bus.

Test sequence

Add one thing, test it, add the next. A fault then has one possible cause instead of eight.

  1. Baseline, nothing attached

    Confirms the rail is clean before you load it.

    python3 bench.py power

    Expect throttled=0x0.

  2. PCA9685 on the bus

    Five wires from the table above. Power off while wiring.

    /usr/sbin/i2cdetect -y 3

    Expect 0x40. A blank grid with the board powered means SDA or SCL isn't landing — check pinctrl get 2,3; both should read hi.

  3. One servo — the result that matters

    Steps in 15° increments. Ctrl-C the instant the wing touches anything. That angle is the travel limit, and it gets hard-clamped in the flight script.

    python3 bench.py sweep P

  4. Did the rail hold?

    Run it again after the servo has moved.

    python3 bench.py power

    0x0 is clean. Bit 0 means the rail is sagging now; bit 16 means it did earlier. Either one is why the 1000 µF caps are in the box.

  5. Second servo, then the strip

    python3 bench.py sweep S python3 bench.py led 144

    Red, green, blue, white. One servo at a time throughout — two MG90S stalling together is ~1.4 A on top of the Pi's 0.35 A against a 1.8 A cell.

If something doesn't work

SymptomLook here first
I²C grid blankpinctrl get 2,3 — either line stuck lo is a wiring fault, not software
Servos twitch, won't turnV+ not connected, or on 3.3 V instead of 5 V
Servo jittersground not shared, or the rail is sagging
Pi reboots when a servo movesbrownout — one servo at a time, then add a cap
Strip completely darkwrong end of the strip, or no common ground
Strip flickers or wrong colours3.3 V logic marginal — this is the case that needs a 74AHCT125

Nothing on this list is damage. All of it is wiring, and all of it is reversible.

GND-01 · DOWNLINK

1.2 m dish · mast-mounted on the 4U rack

The satellite talks to the ground station over plain WiFi, unicast UDP, carrying real CCSDS Space Packets — the same framing a real bus uses, which is what makes the Zeek analyzer meaningful.

Telemetry
UDP 5013 · vehicle → ground
Commands
UDP 5012 · ground → vehicle
Framing
CCSDS Space Packet · 16-byte header
Transport
WiFi, unicast · no broadcast

Packet layout

Verified byte-for-byte against real captures. Note the endianness change at offset 12 — the primary and secondary headers are big-endian, and everything from CCSDS_SPARE onward is little-endian. Getting that boundary wrong is the classic way to decode garbage that still looks plausible.

22CCSDS_SEQUENCEBIG0xC000
42CCSDS_LENGTHBIG85
64CCSDS_SECONDSBIG300
102CCSDS_SUBSECSBIG0
124CCSDS_SPARELITTLE0
16…bodyLITTLE—
TRK-002b

GROUND SEGMENT

4U rack · Raspberry Pi 5 · 'groundation'

A Pi 5 running the whole ground segment: command and telemetry, a protocol analyzer watching the wire, and the detections that come out of it.

Console
OpenC3 COSMOS 7.2.1 + pisat-gsw plugin
Analyzer
Zeek, CCSDS protocol analyzer
Detections
Elastic · SPARTA space-cyber SOC
Host
Pi 5, 8 GB · Ubuntu 24.04

Why a wire tap, not an agent

Nothing is installed on the satellite to catch the attack. Zeek decodes the CCSDS on the wire and ships it to Elastic, so the detection works against a vehicle you do not control and cannot instrument — which is the whole point of the demonstration.

MISSION OPERATOR

Kibana · Attack Discovery

The operator never reads a packet. Attack Discovery correlates what Zeek decoded and names the thing that happened, in the language of the mission rather than the language of the wire.

Critical · 3 alerts

Rogue commanding source targeting CUBESAT-1U. Entities: CUBESAT-1U, GND-01, 10.0.0.75. Contributing detections: rogue commanding source, replayed sequence count.

Then the loop closes: the detection issues a command back to the vehicle, and the wings move on the table in front of you. That visible response is the demonstration — a detection that does something, rather than a row in a table.
